about: The why notes on every exercise card (PLAN 3.5f). A curated, reviewed list: mainstream evidence based training guidance in plain words. Never a person's name or a quote, never a medical claim. A card only ever shows a line from this file; the words in {braces} are filled from the card's own sure data (its name, the muscle it trains, the move it follows or stands in for). 'line' is the card face, 'more' is the two sentences behind the info button.

facts.line: {name} first: you lift the most weight while fresh, the main driver of chest growth
facts.more: Big lifts need the most energy and focus, so they go before anything tires the muscles that help. Take a full rest between sets so every set stays strong.

facts.line: {name} first: your legs are freshest now, so your heaviest sets count most
facts.more: This lift trains your quads and glutes together and asks a lot of your whole body. Doing it first means nothing smaller has tired your legs or your back.

facts.line: {name} first: your back and grip are fresh, so the heavy sets stay solid
facts.more: Hip hinges train your hamstrings, glutes and lower back with a lot of weight. They come before smaller moves so your grip and back are not tired when it counts.

facts.line: {name} first: your back pulls the most while your arms are fresh
facts.more: Rows lean on your biceps and grip, so they go before any arm work. Pull with your elbows and pause for a moment when the weight is closest to you.

facts.line: {name} first: your back does more when your arms are not tired yet
facts.more: Pulling from overhead works the wide muscles of your back, with your biceps helping. Starting here means your arms do not give out before your back does.

facts.line: {name} first: pressing overhead is strongest before your shoulders tire
facts.more: Overhead presses train the front and side of your shoulders, with your triceps helping. They go first so the smaller raises later do not hold the press back.

facts.line: {name} first: one leg at a time takes balance, best done while fresh
facts.more: Single leg lifts train your quads and glutes and even out a stronger and a weaker side. They are harder to steady when you are tired, so they come early.

facts.line: {name} first: your hips are strongest at the start, so the heavy sets count
facts.more: This lift loads your glutes directly with more weight than most small moves allow. Going first lets you push it hard before your legs are tired.

facts.line: {name} first: you lift the most while fresh, and that builds your {muscle}
facts.more: The biggest lift of the workout goes first, before anything tires the muscles that help it. Take a full rest between sets so each one stays strong.

facts.line: {name} first: the biggest lift goes first, while you are fresh
facts.more: The biggest lift of the workout goes first, before anything tires the muscles that help it. Take a full rest between sets so each one stays strong.

facts.line: A second angle for your chest: it works the part your first press reached less
facts.more: Changing the angle of a press moves the work across your chest, so more of it gets trained. You will lift a little less here than on your first press, and that is expected.

facts.line: A second pull from another direction, so your whole back gets worked
facts.more: Rows build the middle of your back and pulling from overhead builds its width. Doing one of each covers your back better than two of the same.

facts.line: A second leg lift that loads your legs a different way
facts.more: Squats lean on the front of your legs and hinges on the back, so one of each trains the whole leg. The second lift is a little lighter because the first did the heavy work.

facts.line: A second press from another angle, so more of your shoulders get worked
facts.more: A different grip or tool changes which part of your shoulders works hardest. You will lift a little less here than on your first press, and that is expected.

facts.line: A second lift for your {muscle}, from a different angle
facts.more: Training a muscle with two different movements works more of it than repeating one. The second lift is a little lighter because the first did the heavy work.

facts.line: A second big lift, from a different angle
facts.more: Training a muscle with two different movements works more of it than repeating one. The second lift is a little lighter because the first did the heavy work.

facts.line: A big lift for your {muscle}: big lifts train the most muscle per set
facts.more: Lifts that move more than one joint work several muscles at once, so they give you the most for your time. They go before the small moves, while you still have energy.

facts.line: A big lift: several muscles work at once, so every set does more
facts.more: Lifts that move more than one joint work several muscles at once, so they give you the most for your time. They go before the small moves, while you still have energy.

facts.line: Finishes your chest: the {lift} did the heavy work, this adds the stretch
facts.more: This move trains your chest through a long stretch without your triceps limiting it. Keep it smooth and stop one rep before your form slips.

facts.line: Finishes the triceps your {lift} already warmed up
facts.more: Your triceps helped on every press, so they are warm and need only a few direct sets. Keep your elbows still and let only your forearms move.

facts.line: Finishes the biceps your {lift} already warmed up
facts.more: Your biceps helped on every pull, so they are warm and need only a few direct sets. Lower the weight slowly, since the way down counts as much as the way up.

facts.line: Builds the shoulder width your {lift} does not reach
facts.more: Presses mostly train the front of your shoulders, and the side gets little work from them. A light weight raised with control is all this takes.

facts.line: Works the back of your shoulders, after the {lift} did the heavy pulling
facts.more: The back of your shoulders helps on every row but rarely gets worked hard by one. A light weight and a short pause at the top is all this takes.

facts.line: Finishes your quads without loading your back again
facts.more: After a big leg lift your back and hips are tired, but the front of your legs can do more. This move works them alone, so you can push close to your last good rep.

facts.line: Works the back of your legs, which the {lift} trains less
facts.more: Your hamstrings bend your knee as well as move your hip, and big leg lifts mostly miss the first job. This move covers it without loading your back again.

facts.line: Finishes the {muscle} your {lift} already worked
facts.more: After a big lift, a smaller move for the same muscle adds work without needing heavy weight. Go close to the point where you could not do another good rep.

facts.line: Trains the side of your shoulders directly, which builds their width
facts.more: The side of your shoulders gets little work from presses, so it needs a move of its own. A light weight raised with control is all this takes.

facts.line: Works the back of your shoulders, which pressing leaves out
facts.more: Most upper body work trains the front of your shoulders, so the back needs its own move to keep up. A light weight and a short pause at the top is all this takes.

facts.line: Trains your {muscle} on its own, so nothing else limits it
facts.more: A small move works one muscle directly, which big lifts cannot always do. Use a weight you control all the way, and go close to your last good rep.

facts.line: A small move that works one muscle directly
facts.more: A small move works one muscle directly, which big lifts cannot always do. Use a weight you control all the way, and go close to your last good rep.

facts.line: Abs go near the end, so they stay fresh to steady your big lifts first
facts.more: Your midsection steadies you in every big lift, so tiring it early makes those lifts harder. At the end it can work as hard as you like.

facts.line: Calves go last: here they cannot hold a bigger lift back
facts.more: Your calves help steady you in every standing lift, so they are trained once those are done. Pause at the top and the bottom of each rep so the muscle does the work.

facts.line: A short finish for your {muscle}, saved for the end
facts.more: Small muscles that help in bigger lifts are trained last, so they never hold those lifts back. A few steady sets are enough.

facts.line: A short finish, saved for the end
facts.more: Small muscles that help in bigger lifts are trained last, so they never hold those lifts back. A few steady sets are enough.

facts.line: Paired with {partner}: one rests while the other works, so you save time
facts.more: These two use different muscles, so doing them back to back costs neither one. Rest once after both, then go again.

facts.line: Part of a round: each move uses different muscles, so you keep moving
facts.more: Doing the moves one after another saves time and keeps you warm. Rest at the end of each round, then start again.

facts.line: A hold for your {muscle}: count the seconds, not the reps
facts.more: Holding still trains a muscle to stay tight, which is the job it has in most lifts. End the hold when your position starts to slip.

facts.line: A hold: count the seconds, not the reps
facts.more: Holding still trains a muscle to stay tight, which is the job it has in most lifts. End the hold when your position starts to slip.

facts.line: Same movement as {from}, so the workout stays balanced
facts.more: It trains the same muscles through the same motion as the move you swapped away. Your sets, reps and rest stay the same.

facts.line: The closest move to {from} your gym has left
facts.more: You have seen every move of the exact same kind this gym has, so this one does the same job as nearly as it can. Your sets and rest stay the same.

facts.line: Instead of {from}: {reason}
facts.more: It is the same kind of movement as the one your plan lists, so the day stays as written. Your plan itself is not changed.

facts.line: A squat: the big lift for the front of your legs and your glutes
facts.more: You bend at the knees and hips together and stand back up with the weight. It trains more muscle at once than almost any other lift.

facts.line: A hip hinge: the big lift for the back of your legs and your glutes
facts.more: You fold at the hips with a flat back and stand tall again. It trains your hamstrings, glutes and lower back together.

facts.line: A single leg lift for your quads and glutes
facts.more: One leg does most of the work at a time, which evens out a stronger and a weaker side. It also asks more of your balance than a squat.

facts.line: A press for your chest, with your shoulders and triceps helping
facts.more: You push the weight away from your chest and bring it back with control. It is the main lift for building your chest.

facts.line: An overhead press for your shoulders, with your triceps helping
facts.more: You push the weight from your shoulders to straight arms overhead. It is the main lift for building your shoulders.

facts.line: A row for the middle of your back, with your biceps helping
facts.more: You pull the weight toward your body and let it out with control. It balances all the pressing you do.

facts.line: A pull from overhead for the width of your back
facts.more: You pull the weight down toward your chest, or yourself up to a bar. It trains the wide muscles of your back, with your biceps helping.

facts.line: A chest move that works it alone, through a long stretch
facts.more: Your arms open wide and come back together, without your triceps doing the work. It is done lighter than a press.

facts.line: A raise for the side of your shoulders, which builds their width
facts.more: You lift a light weight out to the side to about shoulder height. Presses train this part very little, so it has its own move.

facts.line: A move for the back of your shoulders
facts.more: You pull or raise a light weight out and back. It balances the front of your shoulders, which pressing trains a lot.

facts.line: A curl for your biceps, the front of your upper arm
facts.more: You bend your elbow against the weight and lower it slowly. Keeping your upper arm still makes your biceps do the work.

facts.line: A move for your triceps, the back of your upper arm
facts.more: You straighten your elbow against the weight and bring it back with control. Your triceps are most of your upper arm, so they are worth their own move.

facts.line: A move for your quads alone, the front of your thighs
facts.more: You straighten your knee against the weight and lower it slowly. Nothing else has to work, so you can push it close to your last good rep.

facts.line: A move for your hamstrings alone, the back of your thighs
facts.more: You bend your knee against the weight and let it out slowly. It trains a job of the hamstrings that squats mostly miss.

facts.line: A lift that loads your glutes directly
facts.more: Your hips push the weight while your knees barely move. Pause for a moment at the top, where your glutes work hardest.

facts.line: A raise for your calves, the back of your lower legs
facts.more: You rise onto your toes and lower your heels all the way down. A pause at the top and the bottom makes the muscle do the work.

facts.line: A move for your abs, the muscles that steady every lift
facts.more: Your midsection holds your body still or curls it against resistance. A strong midsection helps every other lift you do.

facts.more: It uses only equipment this gym has. Its photo shows the start and the end of one rep.
